claim: Global data centres consumed roughly 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, about 1.5% of world electricity.
notes: Primary intergovernmental estimate. Stated as an estimate with a modelling margin, not a meter reading.

claim: Global data-centre demand roughly doubles to about 945 TWh by 2030 under the IEA Base Case.
notes: Verified as a published scenario. It is NOT a prediction; the IEA publishes multiple cases and the Base Case is only one.

claim: US data centres consumed about 176 TWh in 2023, roughly 4.4% of total US electricity.
notes: National inventory prepared for the US Department of Energy.

claim: US data centres are projected to reach 6.7%-12% of US electricity by 2028.
notes: The range is the finding. Any single-number restatement of this is a distortion.

claim: A single ChatGPT query consumes 500 ml of water.
notes: The source states ~500 ml per CONVERSATION of roughly 10-50 exchanges, and only for specified data centres, seasons and locations. The per-query framing is a compression error introduced downstream.

claim: An LLM query uses about 10x the electricity of a conventional web search.
notes: Traceable to a single 2023 executive remark in S05, not to a measurement. S13 and S14 both report per-query figures broadly comparable to legacy search estimates, so the multiplier is contradicted by later evidence.

claim: Training GPT-3 consumed roughly 700,000 litres of freshwater.
notes: A published modelled estimate under stated assumptions. Never confirmed or denied by the operator. Routinely re-reported as a measurement.

claim: A median Gemini text prompt uses about 0.24 Wh of energy and about 0.26 ml of water.
notes: Self-reported. Methodology is published, but the scope boundary - what is counted in and out - is chosen by the vendor.

claim: AI servers could consume 85-134 TWh per year by 2027.
notes: Peer-reviewed commentary, explicitly framed as a bounded scenario conditioned on production volumes.

claim: Data centres accounted for 21% of Ireland's metered electricity consumption in 2023.
notes: National statistics office. Demonstrates that the global average conceals extreme local concentration - the most policy-relevant finding in the study.

claim: AI will consume 20-25% of US electricity by 2030.
notes: Traceable to an executive interview, not to any national inventory or peer-reviewed model. Directly contradicted by S02's 6.7%-12% range for ALL data centres, of which AI is a subset.

claim: Big-tech data-centre emissions are approximately 662% higher than officially reported.
notes: Depends entirely on market-based vs location-based carbon accounting. Defensible as an accounting critique; misleading when quoted as a measured emissions figure.
